_readme: Expanded versions of Chapter 5-6 content_md. Written fresh, not copied from any source.

sections.5.0:
The last two chapters described how fiat money works. This chapter asks a harder question: what does that system actually cost the people using it?

This isn't abstract. The effects show up in a taxi fare that's gone up again, in a stokvel payout that buys less than it used to, in a family struggling to save no matter how disciplined they are. This chapter names those effects clearly, and shows you the community of people who first organized a serious response.

Before diving into the specific mechanisms, it's worth stating plainly what makes this chapter different from the ones before it. Chapters 3 and 4 were mostly descriptive — this is how money evolved, this is how the fiat system is structured. This chapter is evaluative: given everything you now understand about how the system works, what are the actual consequences for ordinary people living inside it? Holding both a descriptive and an evaluative lens at the same time is a genuinely useful habit for the rest of this Diploma, and for life beyond it. Understanding how a system works is not the same as deciding whether it works well for you — and this chapter is where those two questions finally meet.
sections.5.1:
When new money is created faster than the economy grows, each existing unit of that money buys a little less. This is inflation — and it's not a natural weather event, it's a direct consequence of the fractional reserve and central bank policies covered in Chapter 4.

The painful part is that inflation doesn't hit everyone equally. People holding cash or fixed savings lose purchasing power steadily. People who receive newly created money first — banks, large institutions, asset owners — benefit before prices catch up. Ordinary savers are almost always on the losing side of that timing.

The phrase 'not a natural weather event' is worth taking seriously rather than reading past quickly. Inflation is often discussed in language that makes it sound like an impersonal force of nature — 'prices are rising,' as though prices had independent will. But every mechanism covered in Chapter 4 that increases the money supply is a specific, traceable decision made by a specific institution. This doesn't mean every instance of inflation is deliberate or malicious — sometimes it's a genuine side effect of decisions made for other reasons, like responding to a crisis. But it does mean inflation always has an identifiable cause, and tracing that cause back is far more useful than treating rising prices as simply an unavoidable fact of life, the way you might treat the weather.
sections.5.1.1:
A simple way to feel this: imagine R100 today buys a basket of groceries. If prices rise 10% a year, that same basket costs R110 next year, then R121 the year after — even though your R100 note looks identical.

Activity: try the Effects of Inflation Auction with your group. Watching the same starting amount of 'money' lose real bidding power round after round makes the abstract idea concrete fast.

It's worth extending this same grocery-basket example a little further than the initial illustration, because the compounding effect is easy to underestimate over longer stretches of time. At a steady 10% a year — higher than typical, but not unheard of for periods in various economies — that same basket costs roughly R159 after five years and roughly R259 after ten years. Put differently: money kept as cash under a mattress for a decade, with no inflation protection at all, would have lost more than 60% of its original buying power by the time it was spent, even though the number printed on the notes never changed. This is precisely why the distinction between the number on a banknote and the actual purchasing power that number represents becomes one of the most practically important ideas in the entire Diploma — a distinction Chapter 7 returns to directly when discussing why some people choose to hold a portion of their savings in something other than cash.
sections.5.2: Inflation isn't the only strain on ordinary people in a fiat system. Two connected problems compound it: growing debt at every level of the economy, and a widening gap between those who hold assets and those who don't.
sections.5.2.1:
For an individual, the effect of ongoing inflation is straightforward but serious: money saved under a mattress, or even in a standard bank account, quietly loses value every year it sits there. People who can't afford to buy appreciating assets — property, stocks, Bitcoin — have no way to protect their savings from this erosion. Working harder doesn't fix a problem built into the money itself.

That final sentence deserves to be sat with rather than moved past quickly, because it cuts against a very common and very understandable instinct. Many people, when their savings don't seem to be growing the way they hoped, assume the fault lies with their own discipline or effort — that they simply need to work harder or spend less. Sometimes that's genuinely true. But this section is pointing at something structurally different: even a person who works hard, spends carefully, and saves consistently will still watch their savings lose real value every year they're held purely as cash, purely because of how the monetary system itself is designed. This isn't an argument that effort and discipline don't matter — they clearly do. It's an argument that effort and discipline alone cannot fully solve a problem that's built into the design of the money itself, which is exactly why understanding the system, not just working within it, matters so much.
sections.5.2.2:
At a societal level, the same mechanism widens inequality over time. Asset owners see the price of what they hold rise alongside the money supply, often faster than wages rise for people who don't own assets. The gap between those two groups tends to grow, not because of differences in effort, but because of where each group stood relative to newly created money.

Activity: work through Consequences of the Fiat System with your group — mapping out concretely who gains and who loses at each stage makes this far less abstract.

As you work through the activity, it's worth explicitly naming the two groups this section is comparing, because the comparison is easy to blur into vague talk about 'rich and poor' when something more specific and more mechanical is actually being described. The comparison here is not fundamentally about income level — it's about whether someone's wealth is held in assets whose prices tend to rise with the money supply (property, shares, businesses) versus wealth held in wages and cash, which don't automatically rise the same way. Two people can earn similar incomes and still end up on very different sides of this divide over a decade, purely based on whether one of them was able to convert early income into assets and the other wasn't. This reframing matters because it points toward a specific, mechanical cause for widening inequality, rather than a vague moral story about who works harder — and specific, mechanical causes are the kind of thing you can actually reason about and respond to.
sections.5.2.3:
Governments themselves aren't immune to this dynamic — many carry debt loads that have grown for decades, often serviced by creating more currency rather than fully paying it down. That, in turn, feeds back into the inflation problem covered above. It's a cycle, not an isolated issue.

This cycle is worth tracing through step by step, because seeing it as a closed loop rather than a one-off problem is what makes 'it's a cycle, not an isolated issue' more than just a passing phrase. A government facing a growing debt has, broadly, a few options: raise taxes, cut spending, genuinely grow the economy faster than the debt, or — the option this section is highlighting — create more currency to help cover the gap. That last option provides real, immediate relief for the government's finances, but it also increases the money supply, which by the mechanism covered earlier in this chapter tends to produce inflation. That inflation erodes the real value of the existing debt too, which can look, from the government's side, like a partial solution to the original problem. But it comes at the direct cost of everyone holding that currency, whose savings and wages lose purchasing power in the process. The debt problem and the inflation problem aren't two separate issues happening to coincide — they're mechanically linked, feeding into and reinforcing each other, which is exactly why this section calls it a cycle rather than a list.
sections.5.3: By the late 20th century, a loose community of technologists, cryptographers, and privacy advocates had identified these problems clearly and started asking a pointed question: could money be redesigned so that no single institution held this much power over it?
sections.5.3.1:
This community became known as the Cypherpunks. Beginning in the late 1980s and through the 1990s, they argued that privacy and financial freedom in the digital age would require strong cryptography — tools that didn't depend on trusting a bank, government, or company to behave well.

Many of the technical building blocks Bitcoin would later use were first proposed and debated inside this community, years before Bitcoin existed.

It's worth appreciating just how unusual this community's approach was for its time. Most attempts to fix problems with money throughout history worked within existing institutions — reforming a central bank's policy, changing a law, negotiating a new treaty. The Cypherpunks took a fundamentally different approach: rather than trying to convince existing institutions to behave differently, they asked whether it was technically possible to build systems that didn't require trusting any institution to behave well in the first place — systems where the rules were enforced by mathematics and code, verifiable by anyone, rather than by a promise from an authority. This shift in approach — from 'how do we make institutions trustworthy' to 'how do we build systems that don't require trusting institutions at all' — is the single thread connecting everything in this section to Chapter 6, where that approach finally produces a working result.
sections.5.3.2:
A centralized system has one party (or a small group) making the decisions — creating money, approving transactions, freezing accounts. A decentralized system spreads that authority across many independent participants, with no single point that can unilaterally change the rules or block someone else's transaction.

This distinction is the thread that connects everything so far to what comes next: Bitcoin is, at its core, an attempt to make money decentralized in exactly this sense.

A useful way to test whether you've genuinely internalized this distinction, rather than just memorized the definition, is to ask of any system: if one specific party — one bank, one government department, one company — decided tomorrow to block a particular person from using it, could they actually succeed? In a centralized system, the honest answer is usually yes, at least within that party's own jurisdiction; a bank can freeze an account, a payment processor can decline a merchant, a government can restrict a currency's use. In a genuinely decentralized system, no single party has that unilateral power, because no single party controls enough of the system to enforce such a decision alone. Keep that specific test — could one party alone block this? — in mind heading into Chapter 6, because it's exactly the test Bitcoin's design was built to pass.
sections.5.3.3:
Several attempts at digital cash predate Bitcoin — DigiCash, e-gold, b-money, and others. Each solved part of the puzzle but ran into the same wall: without a decentralized way to prevent someone from spending the same digital money twice (called the 'double-spend problem'), digital cash kept needing a trusted central party after all — defeating the point.

That unsolved problem is exactly where Chapter 6 picks up.

The double-spend problem is worth understanding precisely, because it's easy to underestimate how genuinely difficult it is to solve without a central authority. Physical cash solves this problem automatically, for free, through physics: if you hand someone a R100 note, you no longer physically possess that note, so you cannot simultaneously hand the same note to someone else. Digital information doesn't have that built-in constraint — a digital file can be copied perfectly and sent to two people simultaneously, both of whom would have an identical copy with no way to tell which one is 'real.' Every pre-Bitcoin digital cash system eventually solved this the same way: by appointing one trusted central party to keep the official record of who had spent what, so that party could reject a second attempt to spend the same digital money. That solution works, but it recreates exactly the single point of trust and control that the Cypherpunk movement was trying to escape in the first place. The genuinely hard, previously unsolved problem was finding a way to prevent double-spending without any central party at all — which is the specific technical achievement Chapter 6 explains.
sections.6.0:
In October 2008, a paper titled 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System' was published under the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto — no one knows their real identity to this day. It proposed a solution to the double-spend problem that had stumped every earlier attempt at digital cash, without requiring a trusted central party.

The first Bitcoin block was mined in January 2009. Everything this Diploma has built toward — sound money's properties, the failures of fiat, the Cypherpunks' goals — converges here.

The timing of the 2008 publication is worth noting explicitly, because it wasn't a coincidence. Late 2008 was the height of a major global financial crisis, one that involved bank failures, government bailouts of large financial institutions, and a sharp erosion of public trust in exactly the kind of centralized financial authority Chapters 4 and 5 have spent so much time examining. Whether or not that crisis directly motivated the paper's specific timing, it's a striking backdrop: a proposal for money that didn't depend on trusting banks or governments, arriving at precisely the moment public trust in banks and governments was being tested most severely in generations. From this point in the Diploma onward, every concept from the first five chapters — the properties of sound money, the mechanics of fiat, the specific problems the Cypherpunks identified — becomes a lens for evaluating whether this new proposal actually delivers on what it claims.
sections.6.1:
Bitcoin solves the double-spend problem using a public, shared record of every transaction ever made, called the blockchain. Instead of one company keeping the official ledger, thousands of independent computers around the world each keep an identical copy and agree on updates together.

It's worth pausing on just how different this is from every previous solution covered so far in this Diploma. Every earlier attempt to solve double-spending — including the pre-Bitcoin digital cash systems from the last chapter — relied on reducing the number of record-keepers to one trusted party, on the theory that fewer parties means less coordination difficulty. Bitcoin's approach runs in the opposite direction entirely: instead of minimizing the number of record-keepers, it maximizes them, then solves the much harder problem of getting thousands of independent, mutually distrusting parties to agree with each other anyway. That this is even possible without collapsing into chaos is genuinely surprising, and the next section explains exactly how it's achieved.
sections.6.1.1:
Getting thousands of independent, mutually distrusting computers to agree on a single shared history is a genuinely hard problem. Bitcoin's answer is called Proof-of-Work, part of what's known as the Nakamoto Consensus.

Participants ('miners') compete to solve a computationally expensive puzzle. Whoever solves it first gets to propose the next batch of transactions, and is rewarded with newly created bitcoin for the effort. This makes it expensive to cheat and cheap to verify — the core trick that makes decentralized agreement possible.

That phrase — expensive to cheat, cheap to verify — is worth unpacking a little further, because it's the actual mechanical trick underneath the whole system, not just a slogan. Solving the puzzle requires real computing power and real electricity, spent honestly, with no shortcut. That cost is precisely what makes cheating expensive: to rewrite Bitcoin's history dishonestly, someone would need to redo that same expensive work faster than the rest of the honest network combined, which becomes astronomically costly as more participants join. But checking whether someone else's solved puzzle is valid is almost instant and nearly free for any other participant to verify. This asymmetry — hard and costly to produce, trivial and free to check — is what lets thousands of strangers who've never met and don't trust each other still agree on a single shared history, without needing a referee.
sections.6.1.2:
Several distinct groups keep this system running honestly, each with their own incentives: miners (who secure the network and earn rewards), full nodes (which independently verify every rule is followed, run by anyone), developers (who propose and refine the software), and everyday users (who choose which rules they'll accept by choosing which software to run).

Activity: the Consensus Building activity has your group physically act out how these roles interact — it makes the abstract incentive structure click faster than reading about it.

As you go through the activity, pay attention to a detail that's easy to overlook: no single one of these four groups can unilaterally change Bitcoin's rules on their own, even though each plays an essential role. Miners have significant computing power, but if they tried to enforce rules that full nodes and users rejected, nodes and users could simply refuse to accept their blocks as valid, making that computing power worthless for that purpose. Developers can propose changes to the software, but nobody is forced to run their version — users and node operators choose for themselves. This distributed check-and-balance across genuinely separate groups, each needing the others' cooperation to make any change stick, is a large part of what 'decentralized' actually means in practice, beyond just having many computers involved.
sections.6.2: Chapter 2 laid out the properties good money needs: durability, portability, divisibility, scarcity, fungibility, recognizability. This section asks directly — does Bitcoin actually have them?
sections.6.2.1:
Unlike gold or fiat currency, Bitcoin was designed from scratch with these properties as explicit goals, informed by everything that came before it — including where those earlier forms of money fell short.

This 'designed from scratch, with explicit goals' framing is worth contrasting directly with gold and fiat currency, both of which acquired their monetary properties somewhat by accident of history rather than deliberate design. Gold became money partly because of properties it happened to have as a naturally occurring element, not because anyone engineered it to be ideal money. Fiat currency's properties emerged from a long sequence of historical and political decisions, many made under pressure, rather than a single coherent design process. Bitcoin is unusual in monetary history precisely because its properties — its exact supply schedule, its divisibility, its verification method — were specified deliberately, in advance, by people who had studied exactly what had made or broken earlier forms of money. Whether that deliberate design succeeds is exactly what the next section examines property by property.
sections.6.2.2:
Bitcoin is digitally durable (the network hasn't gone down since 2009), extremely portable (send any amount, anywhere, without physically moving anything), divisible to 8 decimal places (down to a single satoshi, 0.00000001 BTC), and provably scarce — a maximum supply of 21 million coins is enforced by the software every participant runs, not by anyone's promise.

Activity: have the class discussion on whether Bitcoin qualifies as sound money — there's genuine, well-argued disagreement on some of these points worth exploring directly rather than taking as settled.

The phrase 'not by anyone's promise' in the scarcity point is worth returning to directly, because it's the sharpest contrast with every earlier form of money covered in this Diploma. Gold's scarcity comes from geology — nobody promises it, it simply is what it is. Fiat currency's scarcity, to the extent it has any, comes from a policy promise by a central bank, which as Chapter 4 covered, can be changed by that same institution. Bitcoin's scarcity comes from software rules that every single participant in the network independently runs and checks — changing the 21 million limit would require convincing the overwhelming majority of independent participants worldwide to simultaneously adopt different software, something that's happened for far smaller technical changes and met enormous resistance. This doesn't make the limit literally unchangeable in some absolute sense, but it places the decision in the hands of a widely distributed, hard-to-coordinate group rather than a single authority — a genuinely different kind of scarcity than anything examined earlier in the Diploma.
sections.6.2.3:
Bitcoin's design removes the need to trust a central authority — but it replaces that with a different kind of responsibility: yours. There's no bank to call if you lose your private keys or send to the wrong address; no customer service line to reverse a mistake.

This is a genuine tradeoff, not a small footnote. Chapter 7 covers exactly how to hold and use Bitcoin safely, because this personal responsibility is the part most new users underestimate.

It's worth being completely honest about why this tradeoff exists rather than treating it as an unfortunate side detail, because it follows directly and unavoidably from everything covered earlier in this chapter. The entire reason Bitcoin doesn't need a trusted central authority is that no central authority has the power to reverse transactions, freeze accounts, or recover lost access on anyone's behalf — because giving any single party that power would recreate exactly the kind of centralized control the Cypherpunks were trying to escape. You cannot have a system with no single point of control and also have a customer service line that can override that system on your behalf; those two things are structurally incompatible. This is precisely why Chapter 7 treats wallet setup and key management as seriously as it does — not as an optional extra, but as the direct practical consequence of the freedom this chapter has just described.
